title: Division by left multiples in a Frobenius skew-polynomial ring
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-pc-field-characteristic]. Let $A$ be the ring of finite sums $\sum_{i\geq0}a_iF^i$, with coefficientwise addition and multiplication $(aF^i)(bF^j)=a b^{p^i}F^{i+j}$. For a nonzero element $h=\sum_i h_iF^i$, define $\deg h=\max\{i:h_i\ne0\}$. For every $f,g\in A$ with $g\ne0$, there exist $q,r\in A$ such that $$f=qg+r,$$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$. No perfectness hypothesis is imposed on $k$; the quotient multiplies $g$ on the left.

source.place: Printed p.296, paragraph immediately preceding Proposition 14.50: the algorithm called the right division algorithm there, explicitly f=qg+r. Unlike f=gq+r in the final paragraph of that page, this algorithm assumes no perfectness.

proof.text:
Fix $g
e0$ and put $m=\deg g$, so $b=g_m
e0$. Prove the assertion for all $f$ by strong induction on the natural number $N(f)$, where $N(0)=0$ and $N(f)=\deg f+1$ for $f
e0$. If $f=0$, choose $q=r=0$. If $f
e0$ and $\deg f<m$, choose $q=0$ and $r=f$. These choices give $f=qg+r$ and the required remainder condition.

source.place: Printed p.296, right division algorithm immediately before Proposition 14.50; leading-term induction expanded explicitly.

proof.text: In the remaining case let $n=\deg f\ge m$, $a=f_n\ne0$, and $d=n-m$. Since $k$ is a field [def-weil-field], $b^{p^d}\ne0$: if a positive power of $b$ vanished, multiplying by the corresponding power of $b^{-1}$ would give $1=0$. Define $c=a(b^{p^d})^{-1}$ and $u=cF^d$. Expanding the multiplication specified in the statement gives $$ug=\sum_{j=0}^{m}c\,g_j^{p^d}F^{d+j}.$$ Its coefficient in degree $n=d+m$ is $c b^{p^d}=a$, and every coefficient in degree greater than $n$ is zero. This chooses $c$ by inversion in $k$ and requires no extraction of roots.

source.place: Printed p.296, right division algorithm immediately before Proposition 14.50; leading-term induction expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Put $h=f-ug$. The coefficient of $F^n$ is $a-a=0$, and all coefficients above $n$ are zero because this holds for both $f$ and $ug$. Hence either $h=0$ or $\deg h<n$. In either case $N(h)<N(f)=n+1$: for $h=0$ this is $0<n+1$, and otherwise it follows from $\deg h<n$. If $n=0$, the same coefficient calculation says every coefficient of $h$ vanishes, so $h=0$; no degree of zero is used.

source.place: Printed p.296, right division algorithm immediately before Proposition 14.50; leading-term induction expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Apply the strong induction hypothesis to $h$ with the same fixed divisor $g$. It gives $h=q_1g+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<m$. Set $q=u+q_1$. Since $h=f-ug$, distributivity in $A$ gives $$f=ug+h=ug+q_1g+r=(u+q_1)g+r=qg+r.$$ The remainder satisfies the required bound. This completes the induction. In particular $m=0$ forces $r=0$, since a nonzero finite sum has nonnegative degree.
